format

The ape skull as a full-size illustration, and the shard fields it sits beside. Two tasks, one job: make a surface big enough for a poster, a shirt back or a website hero. Both were measured rather than asserted, and both failed once before they passed — and then the first print found a third fault that no measurement was looking for.

Reviewed by the band

The band has now seen this work. Reported 2026‑08‑30: every member read the shared material and looked at the artwork. They like the wordmark, the skull, the year rings and the timeline, and they love the illustrated generated work.

That is a response to a direction, not a signature on each item. Individual artefacts, whether Böbbis becomes a standing per-release character, whether the skull is ever publicly named, and printing or selling anything are all still open. Where a direction was chosen inside a round, that was Marcus’s call.

Start with the plain-language overview if you haven’t already.

01

Where this sits

Two tasks, run together on purpose. 3.2 is the ape skull as a standalone illustration — merch, poster, vinyl label, website hero, print. 3.7 is the production shard fields. They are the same job seen twice: make a surface big enough to carry detail, at the sizes where the mark can finally hold some instead of shedding it.

3.2 also inherits an open question. Round E was asked what the big skull is made of, and failed — it spent its session building a pipeline instead of producing work, and left no folder. The brief for this session made the consequence a rule: judge progress by images on screen, not by tooling built.

The two halves were made in opposite ways, and that was not the plan.

The skull is built from the existing drawing — every version of it comes out of the vector file that already exists, unchanged. It was not redrawn and it was not generated. Same command, same result, every time.

The shard fields are generated images. This task tried twice to build them from scratch in code and both attempts lost to what round C had produced by generating. Marcus called it, the route changed, and section 03 is the account. The consequence worth knowing up front: a new field is a new picture, not a re-run.

02

Not artwork, and not logo files

Nothing in this report replaces anything in assets/logos/. Those are the marks: one colour, two states, no bevel, no gradient, no shadow. These are illustrations, licensed by a separate decision about the skull's job, and the distinction is load-bearing rather than pedantic — section 05 is entirely about what happens when it is ignored.

  • Never place one of these where the glyph goes.
  • Never shrink one. They are drawn for large format and nothing else.
  • Three of the four skull treatments were declined by Marcus on 3 August and are kept only as the record of how the fourth won. Section 05.
  • Some of it has now been on paper — once, on an office printer, and not at full size. That was enough to change two things; it is not a proof, and nothing here has been seen at the size it would actually be used. Section 08.
03

The shard fields

Round C produced shard backgrounds that people liked, as concept images. The standing decision is that the idea ships and those particular files never do: production fields get their own artwork, the exact palette, and a size you can ask for rather than one you crop forever.

This section is not what this task first built, and the corrections are Marcus's. The first version of these fields was grey, and made of flat vector shapes. Both were wrong, and both were caught by comparing them with round C rather than by any check.

Grey. The palette rules cap the warm colour at 2% of any surface, and a gold background is nowhere near that. But that rule was written about a highlight — a hairline, a date, one dot — and had never been asked whether gold can be the ground. Measured, round C's field is 60% gold and the rebuild was 0%. Marcus chose gold, so the rule now carries a written exception with its limits spelled out.

Vector. The standing decision says production fields must be palette-exact. This task read that as must be drawn in vector, which the documents never said, and built two generators that both lost. Marcus: "why can't we generate it as images only, as round C did? I don't understand why a background needs to be vector." He was right — and the honest test was that two rounds of tuning had made the vector version further from the target, not closer, because the constraint was being optimised instead of the picture.

So the fields are generated images, one per shape of surface, and then every pixel is snapped onto the five brand colours. That last step is what makes a generated picture a brand asset rather than a nice picture, and it is measurable:

Raw generationAfter the snap
Distinct coloursthousands5
Pixels off the paletteall of them0
Red — forbidden outright 0.39% – 2.27% 0.000%

The red row is the whole reason that step exists. A generated gold drifts orange every time, and no red anywhere is the oldest rule in the palette. A gold field that has not been through the snap is not a brand asset.

And then the first gold fields were still wrong, twice over. Marcus, looking at them next to his actual favourites from round C: "the generated shards are a bit boring, as they only have one color", and "it would be nice to also have backgrounds without the black hole in the middle."

Both were measurable. His references use cream as a major colour — about 42% of the picture is light. The first fields were 13.6% light and 73% near-black. Worth naming why the checks missed it: they confirmed the field used exactly the five brand colours, which was true, and said nothing about whether it used them. Pale had 1% of the surface. There is a check for that now.

The hole was worth dropping altogether rather than offering as an option. A dark middle baked into the artwork decides forever where a logo may sit, and leaves a hole on anything that does not want one. The dark wash already makes a calm middle when there is type to protect — measured at 6.16:1 on a field with no hole in it at all. So the fields run edge to edge, and the calm middle is added when it is needed.

LightDark
Round C, the reference42.2%37.4%
First shipped field 13.6% 72.9%
The field now 51.7% 27.8%

One thing deliberately not copied: both reference images are skull-and-shards together, and neither skull is the one this brand settled on — one has a pointed crown, the other a full cranium and jaw, both of which six rounds tested and dropped. The layout rules also give a surface one large element, so a shard field is a ground for the word or a title rather than for the skull. The backgrounds were matched; the composites were not. Putting the skull back into the field is possible and would reopen two settled decisions, so it should be asked for rather than slipped in.

One consequence, and it is a rule now

Every surface in this brand gets exactly one warm element — usually a single gold dash a few pixels wide. On a gold field, the field is that element, so nothing else on the surface may be warm and the dash sets in pale grey instead. An amber dash on a gold ground would be both invisible and a second warm element.

Not a new idea — it is the same precedence the brand already uses when the year-by-year activity strip is on a surface: whatever already holds the warmth keeps it, and the dash steps back. The skull posters carry no field, so their dash stays gold.

FieldSizeGoldRedColours
Website hero, 16:93840×216049.9%0.000%5
Square, 1:13000×300052.9%0.000%5
Portrait, 4:52400×300044.9%0.000%5
Poster, A3 at 300 dpi3508×496147.3%0.000%5

One generation per shape of surface, never a crop. Cropping a wide field down to a tall one throws away half the composition and puts the calm centre off-centre. For a size that is not on the list, re-render from the same source; for a shape that is not, generate a new one.

Two smaller things the build settled. A generated image can come back framed — one of these arrived with a paper margin around the artwork, which cannot run to the edge of a poster and is invisible in a thumbnail, so all four edges of every field are now checked. And an AI upscale was not worth it: a 4× pass cost 1 260 credits and, once every pixel had been snapped to five colours anyway, was indistinguishable from a plain resize costing nothing.

04

The scrim gate, which failed first

One requirement has been carried in three documents and demonstrated in none: put a real dark wash behind any type sitting on a shard field. It exists because round C claimed such a wash in its web hero mock-up and never actually built it — the type happened to be legible because the artwork was dark in that spot, which is luck, not a rule.

So this was measured rather than asserted, and measured hard: the contrast of every pixel of every letter against whatever is actually behind it, on both surfaces, with and without the wash — and then the small line slid down each of the four shipped fields in turn, 100 placements in all. One composed picture proves nothing; a single field can pass by accident in exactly the way round C's did.

Going gold made this far more important, not less. Pale letters on a gold shard measure 1.28:1 — worse than any case this check was originally built to catch. On a bare gold field the wordmark, the small line and the date all come out at 1.00:1. That is not hard to read. It is invisible.

The first run failed. Three placements out of 456 came out at 3.47:1, below the 4.5:1 needed for small text. The cause is in the wording of the rule itself: 75% at the centre, radial fixes the value at one point and says nothing about how it fades. Four fifths of the way down a hero, that wash has decayed to 43% — and a pale shard behind pale letters there is unreadable.

The fix: the wash is specified by the type, not by the surface. It is now built to the shape of the letters themselves, at full strength over their own footprint wherever they land, feathered out. The radial one stays on top of it, because that is what makes the middle read as calm.

ScrimWorst subline Placements failing AA 4.5:1
Bare gold field, no wash1.00:1100 of 100
Radial only — the rule as it was written3.47:13 of 456 (on the earlier cold fields)
Radial + foot band + footprint — what was printed, and it was eating the field8.43:10 of 100
Radial at 0.45 + footprint, as it ships now7.27:10 of 100

The middle row is the earlier measurement, on the cold fields, kept because it is what forced the rule to change. The rule used to say 75% at the centre; four fifths of the way down a hero that had already faded to 43%, and three placements came out below standard. The wash is now shaped to the letters themselves.

With the wash, the small line clears the standard at every height sampled, on every field. Without it, every one of the 100 placements fails. That pair is the demonstration the requirement had been waiting for, and it is why the unwashed version is built and kept rather than deleted once it had done its job.

05

The skull, and what it is made of

Structure comes from the existing vector master, unchanged. What was explored is surface: which parts of the drawing stand proud, which are cut away, and what a material does to the light. Four treatments, same geometry, same size.

All four work. Only the engraving shipped, and the reason is a colour rule rather than a preference.

The skull is allowed exactly two colours — pale on dark, or dark on paper, with no third state. Describing a lit surface needs intermediate greys, so every continuous-tone material breaks that rule and cannot avoid breaking it.

Hatching does not, because it makes apparent tone out of two actual colours. An engraved plate is still exactly dark-on-paper. Measured: the two shipped plates contain zero pixels of the third colour; the granite candidates contain over a million.

So the natural-history plate register is not just the one the documents preferred on taste — it is the only one of the four the rules already permit. That is a better argument for it than the one originally made.

06

Two things that looked finished and were not

Both are recorded because in both cases the wrong version rendered cleanly, looked deliberate, and would have shipped.

It came out as chrome first. The first attempt domed each stroke across its full width and let the shading swing the whole range. The result was a soft grey bevelled object — which is precisely the 2011 metal-badge register the rules against bevels and glows exist to prevent. The drawing is a two-tone stencil whose features are holes; carved out of a slab is the only depth reading that does not fight it.

Then it came out flat, and the flatness was a bug being written up as a finding. The shading inside the mark spans a narrow range, so mapping it onto the palette reached only the top two values. The shipped stone plate had three colours in it, one of which was the background; on paper it had two, meaning the object was invisible against the sheet. At thumbnail size it looked like a deliberate flat treatment, and this report had already started saying that continuous-tone materials have nowhere to live on this drawing. They do. The code was not stretching the range. Counting the distinct colours in the output catches it in a second, and the checker now does.

And the surface was lopsided, which Marcus spotted and nobody had questioned. His words: "it looks like there is a skew happening in the mask", and then "it looks a bit busy the more unsymmetric it is." Measured, that turned out to be two separate things. The drawing itself is genuinely not symmetrical — it was drawn by hand and traced, and about 5% of it differs from its own mirror image. That is inherited and nothing here changes it; you cannot see it in the flat logo because a flat colour has nothing to catch light unevenly. But the surface texture was a random pattern with no relationship to the drawing, and that was never a decision — it is what put a pale blotch on one brow and not the other. It is now mirrored, and the light still comes from one side so the object still reads as solid.

Worth recording that the number did not tell the story. On the stone version the asymmetry halved, from 0.30 to 0.16. On the engraved plate the same measurement barely moved — because a diagonal hatch can never mirror onto itself, so the measurement was reading the lines rather than their density. The improvement there is real and it is visible at the brow; the metric simply could not see it. A number can be blind to the thing you changed.

Budget: 2 images, 150 credits, out of roughly 20 000 credits available and 0 used across the whole project before today. Both were prompted for a bare slab with no skull and no text, and both came back wordless. Neither ships, so no commercial-licence claim is being relied on.

07

Where this leaves the open question

Round E asked what the big skull is made of at poster size.

Answered, for the drawn object. Depth is real and reproducible — the sockets read as cut, the strokes as raised, the object has an edge — and material is answered four ways, with the answer being the comparison rather than a sentence.

Two parts are not closed, and neither is claimed:

  • Which register the band uses is Marcus's call, because choosing the carved stone means granting the skull a third colour. The engraving ships because it needs no permission, not because it won a beauty contest.
  • It has now been seen in print, and that answered half of this. The hatched plate was the treatment most likely to change on paper, and it did: it holds at 110 and 70 mm and dies somewhere between 42 and 26. Section 08. What is still unanswered is the register question above, and a real proof on real stock.
08

The first print, and what it caught

On 3 August 2026 Marcus printed all five test sheets on an office A4 machine and photographed them. This is a smell test on one device, not a proof — the photographs below were taken on a desk under a ceiling light, so nothing here settles a colour. It was still worth more than everything that preceded it, because it found two real faults and cleared the two risks the sheets were built to test.

What held. The gold reads as gold. Ink is a deep black rather than a washed grey. Bone separates from Paper easily, which had been listed as a live risk. And the dot texture survived at full size — individual dots resolve, nothing filled in, nothing dropped out. That one was not guaranteed.

The hatch has a floor now

Sheet 02 prints the engraved skull at four widths, and it existed because the width at which the hatching dies on paper was a number this project did not have. It has one. The sheet printed at true size — checked against its own printed labels rather than assumed, with the 110 mm plate measuring 109.3.

Printed widthHatch spacing On the paper
110 mm1.60 mmHolds. Line families read separately.
70 mm1.02 mmHolds. Denser, nothing filling in.
42 mm0.61 mmOn the edge. Reads as texture rather than lines.
26 mm0.38 mmGone. Closed up into a smudge.

The rule: the hatch spacing has to stay at or above about a millimetre on paper — which puts the floor for the engraved plate at roughly 70 mm wide.

Below that, use the flat mark that already exists, the one built and tested across six rounds to survive being made small. No new drawing is needed and none is proposed. Below the hatch floor an engraving is simply the wrong object.

The two bottom verdicts are Marcus's eyes on the paper, not a measurement. The photograph samples the sheet at about ten pixels per millimetre, so at 26 mm the hatch spacing is under four pixels — below what a photograph of it can resolve, whatever the print did. The top two widths the photograph can carry; the bottom two it cannot, and only a person holding the sheet can.

The wash was eating the field

The shard sheets came back with a large soft grey area with no gold and no shard shapes in it — and it was in the artwork, not a shadow: it stops exactly at the edge of the printed area, with clean paper beside it. Marcus found the cause on sheet 01 before any measurement did, by noticing that the strip without text has no dark area and the strip with text does.

The cause was a third dark wash that no document ever mentioned. Alongside the two described in section 04 there was a band running across the foot of the surface at 94% strength, added at some point to help the small line at the bottom and never written down. It was not helping: the record line measured 11.02:1 with it against a requirement of 4.5, and 6.33:1 without. It was buying darkness, not legibility. It has been removed, and the bottom fifth of the poster is back to 52.8% warm — the bare field's own figure.

The obvious repair was tried first and was wrong. Laying a soft wash over the artwork also breaks the five-colour rule the fields are built on, so the wash was snapped back onto those five colours. Every number improved — five colours exactly, and the contrast under the type went up. The picture got worse.

There is no slightly-darkened gold in a five-colour palette. So the soft edge of the wash collapses onto the nearest dark grey and stops being a wash: it becomes a hard-edged dark lozenge sitting behind the words, like a label stuck on the poster. It also cost real gold. The change was reverted, and the pair below is kept as the reason.

One genuine colour fault did come out of it, in a place nobody had looked. Fitting a field to a surface resizes it, and resizing blends colours: the website-sized field was arriving with 33 639 colours before any wash touched it. That is a real breach of the five-colour rule, it had been there the whole time, and the resize now snaps the field back.

And the check that should have caught the band now exists. Everything in section 04 measures contrast under the letters, which is what the requirement asks for — and it passed comfortably while a fifth of the poster went monochrome. The gate now also measures what the wash does to the rest of the picture, band by band down the surface, against the unwashed field. Run against what was printed, it fails.

Printed again — and the new check was blind too

The two changed sheets were reprinted. The fix held: the grey zone is gone from both, the gold runs to the edges, all the type reads, and there is no hard-edged patch anywhere. But with the gold restored around it, something else became visible — the middle of the website-sized version reads as a grey-olive stain.

It is the surface-wide wash, the one the original rule actually asks for, at the strength the rule names. Over gold at 75% it lands on a neutral dark olive: on screen that reads as gold in shadow, on paper it is a dirty patch. The poster does the same thing arithmetically and does not show it, because that artwork's middle is already dark where the wash sits — which is the whole reason one sheet looked wrong and the other did not.

And the check added one step earlier could not see it. It reported 58.3% before the wash and 58.3% after on a surface whose centre had gone from gold to grey. It was counting pixels by hue, and darkening something does not change its hue — only how much colour is left in it. It caught the foot band only because that wash was violent enough to drain the colour entirely.

It now measures how much red there is over blue, which is the actual question and collapses exactly as a wash darkens. Re-run against the sheet that was printed, the poster's bottom fifth scores 3.7% of a bare field and fails.

That is three measurements in this round that were blind to the thing they were watching — the symmetry number in section 06, the colour count above, and this one. They share a shape: each measured something that survives the change being tested. It is worth stating as the round's most transferable lesson, because it will happen again.

It ships at 0.45 instead of the 0.75 the original rule names, on both surfaces. The rule's intent — a real wash, and a calm centre for the type — is met; its number was written when the backgrounds were cold and was never revisited when they went gold. The departure is recorded at the setting itself rather than left for someone to rediscover. The poster could have kept the higher value since it hides the problem, and did not: two undocumented numbers is how a brand drifts.

09

Method, and what the evidence cannot show

  • The skull is fully re-runnable — same command, same files, structure from the unchanged vector master. The shard fields are not: their sources are generated images, kept in the folder and labelled as such, and a new generation is a new picture rather than a re-run. That is a real difference from every other asset in this brand and it is a consequence of the route Marcus chose.
  • Every shipped surface was read back off disk and checked against the colour rules: no red, one warm element, the accent under its ceiling, the right warm colour for the ground, nothing warm touching the skull. Twelve surfaces, clean, plus three declared exceptions.
  • Generations used: 25 images and one upscale, 3 075 credits of roughly 20 000. Every one was prompted with no text, no skull and no figures, and every one came back that way. About two thirds of that spend is the cost of getting the fields wrong twice — the four that ship cost roughly 300 credits. Worth saying plainly rather than presenting the total as the price of four backgrounds.
  • Licensing — read, and it does not cleanly pass. While nothing generated shipped this was moot; the shard fields changed that. The generator's own terms allow commercial use on a paid plan, but on merchandise sold to multiple buyers its content "must be a secondary element of the design — not the main visual focus", and the merchandise licence that lifts that restriction "covers non-AI Premium files only. AI-generated resources are excluded." Website, social and unsold posters are fine. A shard field as the whole graphic on a shirt appears not to be covered, and a trademark application is not addressed at all. Three routes are recorded; this needs a qualified opinion rather than a designer's guess.
  • The five sheets were printed on 3 August 2026 — section 08. One office A4 machine, photographed on a desk. Still no press and no proof, and the difference matters: it was enough to catch a dead grey zone and to give the hatch a floor, and nowhere near enough to settle a colour.
  • Two colour findings are recorded and deliberately not acted on. Aged Brass read more olive than brass, and Ink barely separated from Slate — which matters, because Slate's job is raised panels and a panel that close to the ground is invisible. Neither can be settled on an uncalibrated office printer, and acting on either would be guessing.
  • The A3 sheets were printed on A4, so even the print was at 71% of size. Nothing has been seen at full physical size, on a wall or on a shirt.
  • The shard poster still names the band twice — once as the wordmark and again in the line at the foot. The same fault was caught and fixed on the skull poster; this surface never got the same treatment. Visible on the printed sheet, and open.
  • The legibility standard is a floor, not a design goal. The gate proves the small line is readable. Whether the hero reads well at a glance is a judgement, and the answer to that is the pictures.
  • The gate tested one line of text, at one size, centred. A longer line, a left-aligned one or a paragraph would need re-measuring.
  • Four fields is four files, not a range. A fifth field is an untested picture until the checks and the gate have been run on it.
  • A measurement was thrown away. The first version of the height sweep took the worst pixel in each row rather than following the actual letters. It sounded more rigorous and was useless — one bright splinter anywhere in the row pinned the score, so the washed and unwashed results came out identical.
  • The band has not seen any of this.
